speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to be able to respond to the Speech from the Throne and particularly to the first part of that speech which deals with peace-keeping. This has been a great concern of mine over the last four or five years and particularly over the last two years. I am very proud to be able to associate myself with members from both of the other Parties in a minority report which 1 believe in very strongly as the eventual solution to our problems.
Mr. Speaker, over the last few years I have come to conclude that a nuclear exchange in this decade is a strong possibility and that the consequences of that exchange would be that civilization as we know it would perish. 1 believe that is what is in store for humanity on this globe, and particularly for the people in the northern hemisphere. It is not simply a matter of something which will occur between the Soviet Union and the United States; it is something that will happen to all of us.
In the last couple of weeks over 100 million Americans and Canadians witnessed the film "The Day After". We saw the result of that nuclear exchange. I have not used the word "war" in terms of that exchange because I do not think we are talking about a war. We are talking about "nuclear omnicide". A war is something that one side or the other can win or one side or the other will lose. There is some expected political or economic gain which would occur from a war, but we are talking about something that would be the end of it all for virtually all of us. We saw that in the film The Day After. If you watch the film you see the horrendous consequences of a nuclear attack, Mr. Speaker.
[DOT]	(1110)
Some might say that this only concerns the United States because Canada does not have nuclear weapons or is getting rid of them; therefore we will not be part of it and it will not affect us. Of course, that is incredibly wishful thinking because
in the first wave, as we saw in Lawrence, Kansas, the first thing that would be attacked would be Minuteman silo bases and the Trident submarine bases which would be used to destroy the other side, the Soviet Union. The first attack would be an attempt to destroy those silos of which there are hundreds throughout the northern United States close to the Canadian border.
The Canadian Public Health Association has shown that half of the people in most of the cities in the West, from Vancouver right through to the East and certainly to communities like Thunder Bay, would die from the fallout of these blasts. Each silo would likely be subjected to 25 times the size and power of the bomb used at Hiroshima. In the first round alone, probably somewhere around seven million or eight million people in Canada will die.
In addition, Canadians would be subject to certain types of bombing because there are targets in our country of significance to an enemy even if we were not involved. One of those targets is airports with runways longer than 10,000 feet because they would be places where B-52 bombers could land after an attack.
The Canadian Public Health Journal says that 12 million or 13 million Canadians would die in the first round and as a result of its consequences. In all of the wars in which Canadians have been involved, we have only had approximately
125,000	casualties. Consider that in the first few days of a nuclear exchange involving North America, half of all Canadians would die. That is why I consider this topic to be the most important one to discuss. That is why I am pleased that the first issue raised in the Throne Speech was this event which could very well occur.
Further to the kind of information we have had about fallout radiation and so on, we have seen a far worse scenario which was developed by U.S. scientists, particularly at Harvard but which has been concurred in by different scientists around the world, including those in Russia who say that their findings are the same. Let me quote from a short article just to describe the other consequences of such an exchange:
The Soviet scientists said their own studies confirmed recently published American findings-
These are the American findings.
-that an exchange using only a small fraction of existing warheads would produce a 'nuclear winter' in which smoke and soot obscured sunlight, temperatures plunged to below freezing levels even in summer, food crops and other ecological systems were wiped out, radiation was several times more intense than previously estimated and, when the pall lifted, ultra-violet rays from the sun reached untenable levels.
That is what the Americans said, "using only a small fraction of existing warheads". The article goes on:

The Russians said their research indicated additional catastrophic consequences, including the creation of a global 'toxic smog', unchecked biological epidemics, a substantia! depletion of the earth's oxygen supply and-
And this is terribly important,
-the probable shattering of the interconnecting web of systems that sustain life on the planet.
I believe this is what is in store for us if we do not make some very major changes. However, many people say that this will not happen, that the superpowers or political leaders will not allow it, and that while the danger is ever great it will not happen and we can be fairly sure that we will all survive. The superpowers and the political leaders would not want or cause this to happen; but there are a whole series of scenarios which one could write whereby this could happen, almost as if by accident.
U5)
I would like to look at a couple of scenarios because it is tremendously important when we are dealing with this issue to realize that the danger is great and that what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and others are attempting to do is vital. I could refer to the situation in the Middle East, a crisis in Europe, in West Berlin or something of that nature. Perhaps a crisis in the Middle East is far more possible than we might have concluded in the past. If the situation reached the point where one side or the other decided that a nuclear war could happen in a very tense situation, possibly with some other kind of ongoing conventional warfare, if one side decided that the other side would strike first, there is always the danger of a pre-emptive strike of weapons which can destroy the enemy silo before one can fire its warhead. That is always a strong possibility in any major crisis.
Perhaps there is even a stronger possibility when we talk about weapons like the Pershing 2, the MX and to some extent the SS-20, although it is a much older weapon, that these weapons could evoke a launch on warning response. The Pershing 2 could be deployed in West Germany close to the border with East Germany. This particular weapon would take anywhere from six minutes to ten minutes to go from launch to target. The time is very, very short and crucial. There have been hundreds of occurrences where computers mistakenly have misread some danger or that a particular warhead was coming, but these have been corrected. Six, eight or ten minutes is not time enough for correction, so the Soviets have threatened-and the Americans have talked about the same thing-a response known as launch on warning. If a computer error occurs and a flock of geese is misinterpreted as a warhead, if one has only six minutes to ten minutes to check it out, then one launches on warning. That is what is going into play at this very moment as these weapons are being deployed.
There are various possibilities, although I have only mentioned one. We have a large number of our warheads in submarines at sea. In each submarine there are two people whose job it is to fire the weapons. They cannot be fired unless the two of them do it. Each has been sworn to kill the other if one should try to do it on his own. Suppose the two of them, having been at sea for three months or four months-and I
have been at sea for 30 days or 40 days and I know that one can become a little strange over that period of time-decided to fire the weapon, one Poseidon submarine has 160 warheads which can destroy 160 Soviet cities. With the Trident submarines coming along, they have something close to 200 warheads. God knows what the Russians have, but this is the kind of thing that can occur. I list these few examples only to show what could happen.
Then there is the example of a decapitation strike; that is, to destroy the enemy command post. A small war could become much larger because there would be no one to restrain those who would fire at will. Unless we get control of this situation, this nuclear exchange will occur with all of the consequences that I have mentioned.
There is a myth that the Soviets are much stronger than we are, and therefore we have to become stronger. All evidence, including the Scowcroft Commission, the Pentagon and other military people, shows that we are far stronger than the Russians. There is general parity, but in most areas our side, including the Americans, is well ahead. We are ahead where it counts. For example, the Russians have far more land based strategic ICBMs, 5,500 to 2,100, but we have $,700 to 1,970 sea based missiles, and the sea based missiles cannot be destroyed in a first strike.
It would take me another half hour to develop this subject of weaponry. I would like to do so as it is tremendously important, but times does not permit. I repeat, there is general parity, but where it really counts, our side is better protected. The myth that we are about to be destroyed by the Russians, that we are much more vulnerable, is just that-a myth.
I wish to say a few words about what the Prime Minister is attempting to do. I admit that this will sound partisan but I do not know of any leader of a middle power who has the ability to do what he is attempting to do. I have spoken with high-ranking military people, not just Canadians, who have had conversations with him. I brought Paul Warnke the Chief SALT negotiator, to see him a year ago. Everyone is amazed at the knowledge which the Prime Minister has on this subject. It is a very complex subject and he is extremely knowledgeable. A very high level American general stated that he has not met any other political leader and only a few military people who have that knowledge.
This is exceedingly crucial when dealing with this matter. You have to know the situation. I do not think the Canadian people are aware of the degree to which the Prime Minister is so well informed. In the conversation with Mr. Warnke the Prime Minister said he was not as well versed as he should be. However, the two of them talked for an hour and a quarter as virtual experts. This is what we need.
The other factor is that the Prime Minister knows many people around the world. He has been a political leader longer than anyone else. It is important that he continue and complete the project.
December 12, 1983

There are four very important points in this project. I wish to deal with the last point, stability. There is a great deal of instability. 1 have indicated how a nuclear war could start, partly because of the weaponry. The Prime Minister is very concerned that stability be maintained and increased. We must stop building such destabilizing weapons as the Cruise missile, for example. We must do something about the very serious situation involving destabilizing weapons such as the Pershing 2 and the MX. We should attempt to stop the development of these things and we are very conscious that we must move into a new phase in this matter in order for the world to become a much more stable place to live.
We cannot get rid of nuclear weapons immediately. We can put a freeze on them, but in one way or another we must do something about those elements which are far more destabilizing than others and those are some of the things that the Prime Minister has been talking about.
1 believe there is now a period of time allowed for questions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to represent the constituents of Provencher and my Party by replying to the Throne Speech. The theme of the Throne Speech, peace and prosperity, is both seasonal and laudable. The script writers are obviously more attuned to the times than the principal actors who are supposed to act upon the Throne Speech. The principal actors, those opposite us, obviously had a major input in it, because what at first seems to be seasonal yule tidings is, on reflection, clearly Liberal pre-election strategies and tithings.
The Liberal message is simple: "Buy our Throne Speech, vote for us and good times will continue". That is the same old message from the same old Government with the same old pre-election schemes and promises. Indeed, the Throne Speech confirms that the Government is competent only in the area of promises and platitudes.
Some good programs have been promised, and as the Leader of my Party said on Friday, these programs will be supported. However, Canadians have seen the Government in operation long enough. Hence, they seriously question which programs will be adopted and worry about the form those programs will take. Additionally, they are concerned about the time that will be needed to put those programs in the form of legislation.
The public is gravely skeptical of the Government. That is the tragedy of the situation, Mr. Speaker. Even potentially good policies are jeopardized with this Government in power because it has made the Canadian public so suspicious. The Throne Speech has not changed the public's perception of the Government. In short, the Government has lost public confidence.
The Address-Mr. Epp
Most Hon. Members in the House lost confidence in the Government long ago. Some Liberal members who are more openly honest than others have also made their views known. If those members along with others would let their conscience be their guide and their constituents be their primary concern, this Parliament would respond this week to the public's wishes with a vote of non-confidence in the Government.
During his speech on Friday, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that our Party was reactionary. Yes, Mr. Speaker, we along with the majority of Canadians, over the last 20 months, have reacted to a government marked by economic mismanagement, a government marked by complacency, a government full of avarice, a government known for its arrogance, a government that has shown a lack of concern with Canadians' reactions to Revenue Canada's tactics, a government that is cynical toward those who elected it. Yes, we are reacting, along with the majority of Canadians, to a government that promises lower energy costs, lower inflation, lower interest rates and then produces just the opposite.
I know that the Liberal back-benchers wanted and needed, during the Christmas recess, to be able to scurry hither and thither in their constituencies proclaiming the Throne Speech as Liberal gospel, selling bits and pieces of the Liberal tithes and insisting that they had experienced certain new revelations. The Prime Minister, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) have all participated in what has been euphemistically referred to as the big lie. For example, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said on Friday, as reported at page 50 of Hansard:
Let me tell all those Canadians out there who think it is time for a change that if they elect a Tory Party they had better not be sick.
That is what the Prime Minister said. That comment drew my thoughts back this weekend to George Orwell's book 1984. In that book a new language would be used called newspeak or minitruth. Public statements would be announced from a pyramidal waste concrete structure rising 300 metres into the air. Of the three principles of newspeak, one of them was "ignorance is strength". The Government has already perfected newspeak-keep people in the dark and only let them see and hear what is favourable to the Government. Newspeak is not designed only to keep people uninformed, Mr. Speaker, but to develop a second theme and that is doublethink. It has never been better said than it was by the author, and I quote:
The Ministry of Peace concerns itself with war: the Ministry of Truth with lies; the Ministry of Love with torture and the Ministry of Plenty with starvation. These contradictions are not accidental nor do they result from ordinary hypocrisy. They are deliberate exercises in doublethink-
And now comes the important statement:
For it is only by reconciling contradictions that power can be retained indefinitely.
No matter what you have to say, no matter what you have to do, the point of the Prime Minister's actions is to stay in power. That is the theme of the Throne Speech.

December 12, 1983
The Address-Mr. Epp
With those revelations in sight the Liberals have vowed to make amends. A fitting penance, in my view, would be banishment to political oblivion as judgment day approaches for that entire lot. Among their biggest crimes in my mind and in the minds of many Canadians is their use of medicare as a political football. Much to their chagrin, no one has taken them up on their dare to kick that football or reacted to their taunts designed to draw somebody offside so that they can pick up that football and run to an election with it. Their major concern is not medicare, it is what I quoted earlier, to stay in power indefinitely. This is one of the vehicles they want to use.
The reason no one has kicked that football or gone offside is that all Canadians support medicare. Certainly everyone in the Progressive Conservative Party supports medicare and will continue to support it. Make no mistake about that, Mr. Speaker. It was this Party while in government in 1979-and I could go back to the period of the Right Hon. John Diefen-baker as well-that commissioned the father of medicare, Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, to undertake a review to ensure that it was sound. In his report Mr. Justice Hall indicated that he had, and I quote:
-found no one, not any Government or individual, not the Medicare profession nor any organization not in favour of Medicare.
That group includes the progressive Conservative Party and nothing has changed, absolutely nothing.
The Throne Speech failed to make an important distinction which needs to be made for parliamentarians and the general public and that is that medicare on the one hand and the Liberals' proposed health care Act, which I hope comes in today, on the other, are two entirely separate things. They are not, I repeat, one and the same. I will explain that. If we keep this distinction in mind then we will have a more reasoned analysis of what the Government's proposed legislation might contain and how it can be improved without the hysteria and fear that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has tried to generate. She has already spent nearly a quarter of a million dollars trying to convince Canadians that a crisis exists. Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to look at her own polls which show that there are a number of issues well ahead of that concern. I say to Hon. Members opposite that from our perspective medicare is good; medicare must be kept; medicare must be fostered and it must be enhanced.
If the Liberals' proposed Health Care Act contains provisions that maintain and foster medicare, we will be the first to support it, along with others in the House. We, along with millions of Canadians, have been anxious to see that legislation and I understand that it will be brought in later this day.
In the past several months provincial ministers have requested that federal representatives meet with them to discuss this issue. The Government has steadfastly refused and I will give you one example of this. There was a meeting of health ministers in Halifax in September. The Minister did not go there to consult, she went there to insult, Mr. Speaker. That is a strategy which she is still following, today. Then, in selfrighteous indignation she huffed back to Ottawa proclaiming in this House that "the meeting was quite a waste of time".
Indeed, if it was a waste of time that was due to her continued unwillingness to listen. That indeed has wasted a lot of good time.
The provinces wanted to discuss underfunding and they wanted to talk about medicare. The Minister told them that she was not going to discuss the funding side of medicare. We have seen the Minister of National Health and Welfare running around the country like a cannon that has lost its moorings on the deck. She is going hither and yon, shooting here and shooting there, but about all she is doing is hitting herself in the foot.
The unwillingness to act among Ministers in the Government probably stems in part from the Prime Minister's conviction, which he stated earlier this year, that co-operative federalism is dead. If it is dead, Mr. Speaker, Canadians know who killed it. In the Throne Speech the Government proclaims that it wants to resuscitate the corpse. In the Throne Speech we read that the Government intends to introduce more permanent mechanisms of consultation. Is it the mechanism or the attitude of this cast of actors at the federal level that has failed in the past? I put it to you and to all Canadians, Mr. Speaker, that it is the latter. No amount of new mechanisms can change that. What is needed is a change of personalities that have the trust and confidence of the Canadian people and who understand co-operative federalism.
Even in the Throne Speech the Government has found it hard to be honest with Canadians. Over the past several days it has had to adjust several figures and concede that many were nothing more than half-baked statistical information and manipulations. This was particularly true of the statistics concerning health, welfare and post-secondary education.
First, it was trying to take credit for money which legally belonged to the provinces under contractual obligations it signed under the Established Programs Financing agreements. Second, it tried to give the impression, at least, that most of the money was discretionary, so-called new money, and subsequently the Minister of Finance had to admit that none of it was discretionary and that it indeed legally belonged to the provinces.
Third, in the Throne Speech the Government told us the amount involved was $500 million, but the Minister of Finance goes to Montreal, a mere 100 miles away, and suddenly, on the road there, finds another $269 million. The Government cannot even get its facts straight any more. Are the Canadian people expected to believe that the federal Government did not know about this beforehand-that the Throne Speech suddenly made this revelation and the next day, within 100 miles, on the road to Montreal, it just happened to find another $269 million? Who is it trying to kid? The Minister of Finance is developing a reputation for marginal adjustments of $200 million or more since his last budget speech.
The fourth manipulation is that Ministers have also tried to leave the impression that the sum to be transferred to the provinces in entirely targeted for health care. They know and we know that is not the case. In their public statements they should make clear what those amounts are and not leave in the
December 12, 1983

Throne Speech the statement that this is an example of the federal Government's strong support for medicare and the funding thereof.
The fifth manipulation is the deliberate attempt to create the impression that this increased money going to the provinces, which legally belongs to them anyway, is somehow guaranteed on a long-term basis. It is not, Mr. Speaker; it is only for 1983-84. Future sums are subject to fluctuations in the economy and the GNP. If the economy falters, so does that money and so does the funding of medicare. The Government had better understand that.
The sixth and to my way of thinking by far the gravest fact that these Ministers try to hide is that the new sum does not take into consideration the estimated $5.8 billion-count it, Mr. Speaker, $5.8 billion-less than what the provinces anticipated from 1982 to 1987 under EPF. The reason for the shortfall is that in 1981 there was a change, a formula alteration, a loss of the revenue guarantee. That unilateral action is causing tremendous difficulties, especially in those provinces where 50 per cent of the income is federal transfer payments. Do they want to stand here today and say that the Premiers of Atlantic Canada are mean spirited and do not know how to run their medicare programs? That is not the case.
I know the Premiers met as recently as ten days ago and one Atlantic premier said he needed $150 million right now just for medicare. Another one said $200 million. Another one estimated $150 million. Prince Edward Island estimated $40 million. When you add up those numbers you are already in excess of $500 million but this Government goes to Halifax and will not even discuss it. That is what happened and they had better understand that.
The Speech from the Throne says, Mr. Speaker, that legislation will be introduced to increase the supplement for single pensioners. I understand the task force on pension reform must report by December 31 of this year but likely will report earlier. We urge the Government to make an early response to the recommendations of the task force which will directly help those below the poverty line, those who need an increase in the GIS to retain the dignity that the elderly of Canada are entitled to. The same applies especially to any provisions for widows and widowers between the ages of 60 to 64.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, I will say more when the Canada Health Act comes before us, but part of the Government's strategy is that somehow Conservative provincial governments are mean spirited. Well, I want to give an example of what has happened in Winnipeg with an NDP government in charge. The Health Sciences Centre is our largest hospital in that province. Two infants died in that hospital and Mr. Justice Gyles delivered a report on that situation. I do not want to be misinterpreted in any way, Mr. Speaker. I am not blaming the Government of Manitoba for those deaths and I want that very clearly understood. But what is interesting is that, yes, it is conservative provinces and NDP provinces that want to discuss
The Address-Mr. Epp
underfunding because they are all facing the same problem. It has nothing to do with partisanship or the political philosophy of the party.
1 have before me today an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press headlined "Nurses Complain of Staffing Shortages" in the Health Sciences Centre. They want to meet with the provincial Minister of Health, the Hon. Larry Desjardins, to discuss these issues. These are the issues that must be discussed, Mr. Speaker. The issue of changes from acute care to home care, to community care and preventive health care. The list goes on and on and we will expand on it in the debate on the Canada Health Act. But I want to say that Canadians support this program; and I say to the Prime Minister and his supporters, yes, let us have a spirited debate but let us stay with the facts.

Mr. Speaker, 1 pointed to that case as an example of what is happening.
Lastly, the Minister bases much of her argument on the fact that she has experienced tragedy which has moulded her thoughts and attitudes. I respect her experiences but I tell her that Liberals do not have the exclusive right to compassion. It is not the exclusive right of any party or person. All members in this House, everyone in society, has or will experience in his or her family's lifetime joy and sorrow, life and death. I know the Minister is aware that illness touches everyone. Oh yes, some of us can speak of those experiences as well. 1 can speak as a father who took his infant daughter to her grave. All I am saying, Mr. Speaker, to the Government is this: "When we deal with medicare, deal with the facts, and we will deal with you".

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) a couple of questions concerning the deteriorating health standards in Manitoba under the NDP government. The situation has become quite tragic and there is legitimate concern, as my colleague has outlined.
We know that control of the Deer Lodge Hospital was transferred to the government in April of this year and it received considerable funding to bring it up to proper standards, but the money has not been properly utilized. There are hundreds of beds available, but there is just a trickle of patients going in. There are line-ups at every other hospital in Manitoba of patients trying to get operations. Would the Hon. Member recommend that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) launch an investigation as to why that hospital is not being properly utilized?

December 12, 1983
The Address-Mr. Epp
I would also like to ask him about this regressive payroll tax which the NDP have in Manitoba. The hospital administrators have stated that the 1.5 per cent payroll tax is killing them. Would the Hon. Member recommend that the Minister take a look at this disastrous situation in Manitoba and have her recommend to the NDP government that it remove this regressive payroll tax and launch an investigation to see if all health care funds are being allocated for health care in the Province of Manitoba?

Mr. Speaker, in reply to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie), I think all members are aware of the transfer from the federal Government to the provincial government. I have had a number of representations from veterans' organizations, both collectively and individually, who would like Deer Lodge to be utilized more for their use. There is a special concern for people who have had a long wait to get into Deer Lodge, and that obviously should be discussed as well as the whole matter of transfers of federal veterans' hospitals to the provinces.
With regard to the payroll tax, there is no doubt that hospital administrators and others in similar institutions, for instance university presidents, feel that this tax has created a very serious difficulty not only in cash flow but also regarding their ability to hire people. That is one reason some hospital administrators give for certain positions not being filled, They just do not have the money from the funding of the provincial government and the 1.5 per cent payroll tax is possibly hurting more than the revenue gained. The impression is left that the government is anti-jobs. It is also pointed out very clearly by investors and others that the 1.5 per cent payroll tax is a tax which people cannot understand. Why do they have to pay a tax when they create a job? They have to pay 1.5 per cent of the gross payroll of any company. Every hospital, every university and every school board has to do that. Mr. Speaker, this has seriously affected job creation in the provinces.
The last point the Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) made was on the question of whether health care funds from the federal Government to the provinces were being diverted to purposes other than health care. The best evidence I have there, Mr. Speaker, is the report of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall. He was asked to investigate that question, among others, and he said he had found absolutely no evidence that there was diversion of those funds.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with care to the Hon. Member's comments. 1 have great respect for his compassion on the subject. There are two questions I would like to raise with him. When he talks about the money that the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) indicated would be available to the provinces over and above the standard block funding because of the way the calculations were made in the past, is it his contention that the provinces had budgeted this money already because they knew it was coming, and that therefore when the provinces talk about underfunding by the federal Government they had already
calculated receiving this money and the underfunding was with that in mind? Where does the Member personally stand on the question of user fees and extra billing?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that those questions were asked and the manner in which they were asked by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans). It is now established that we are talking about $769 million. The $769 million flows directly from what is known as the Established Programs Financing formula. There has been debate for some period of time between the provinces and the federal Government. The provinces said they were not receiving the money which the formula should be giving to them, even the formula that they had not agreed to, as you recall, in the negotiations that took place in 1981. They thought that the formula itself was giving them more money.
I obviously cannot speak for every province, but I can speak from some discussions I have had with them. They will obviously have spoken for themselves when they were in Montreal last week with the Minister of Finance. There is no question that they thought more money was coming from the formula. Their concern is that while the federal Government says it is supporting 50 per cent of medicare, that is acute care hospital costs and medical costs, so many other programs, which are both needed and can take people out of high cost, acute care hospital beds, are not being cost shared. Their argument is, why can we not look at those areas? Why is the federal Government so narrow on its 50 per cent? Should we not look at those areas and see if we cannot target some of the additional money for those areas to remove people from acute care hospital beds? Our Leader has been saying very directly that that is what this Party would do. 1 would like to speak more on that when the Canada Health Act is before us.
On the point of user fees and extra billing, our Party has come out quite strongly federally saying that we do not support user fees. 1 will also indicate very quickly that there are various kinds of user fees. 1 do not have time to discuss that.
The Member for Kitchener (Mr. Lang) smiles. He is a doctor. I guess I will have to discuss that because I do not want him to misinterpret again. For instance, there are people in chronic care hospitals, as he should know, most of whose pension money goes for the maintenance of that facility and the services provided. I take it when we talk about user fees that that is not what we are talking about, unless the Member for Kitchener sees it otherwise as a medical doctor. I take it what we are talking about when we speak of user fees is people coming into acute care hospitals and emergency wards, for example. We said we do not support that. If the Member for Kitchener has any other thoughts he can enlighten us.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we fight our way out of the recession there are a lot of tough questions facing Canadians today. Must this happen again? Are we forever doomed to be sort of a coat tails economy, depending on others for our prosperity? Or can we do something really different? Is there a bold new course that we can take as a nation to build a brighter future for ourselves and our children? There most certainly is.
Nature has provided Canada with a priceless key to its own economic salvation. With this jey we can both unlock the doors of our dungeon of economic dependency and offer world leadership in a crucial area of global concern to bring fresh hope to humanity's hungry millions. This key is water, the white gold of the 21st century. Through imaginative, efficient management of this most precious resource we can generate wealth. We can create and sustain a vast range of new and meaningful jobs for Canadians and we can enhance the overall quality of life on this continent from the Arctic circle through to the heartland of Mexico. All the ingredients are at hand. We have the resources, the technology and a heaven sent geographic blueprint for success. What we need is the vision to grasp this opportunity and the will and courage to transform it into concrete reality.
Let us take a look at what we have. Canada enjoys a greater abundance of water wealth than any other nation on earth. With well under 1 per cent of world population, we have more than one-quarter of all the global reserves of fresh water. This accident of nature has shaped our history. Its enormous potential somehow fails to occur to us in our normal planning for the future. Unless we wake up and realize all the implications of this position in today's world, realization will very soon be thrust upon us.
Across the world, inequitable distribution of water lies at the root of untold human hunger and misery. As we approach the crossroads of the year 2000, the stark reality carries the seeds of mounting international tensions and the risk of global conflict. On our own continent the crisis is not so acute but the same pattern of inequitable distribution is evident. More than 90 per cent of Canada's population is concentrated in a 300-kilometre strip along the Canada-U.S. border. Yet over 60 per cent of the fresh water flow of our mighty rivers is northward. Thus, every day these northern rivers pour countless millions of gallons of pristine pure water into the salty Arctic sea. At the same time our Great Lakes are desperately in need of flushing with fresh supplies. Our agriculture is threatened in a growing number of areas across the country, industrial development is curtailed or halted by lack of water availability and we have a mounting pollution problem.
The magnitude of the water problem in Canada's West was pointed out a couple of weeks ago in a brief to the Royal Commission on Economic Union by the Minister of Agricul-

December 12, 1983
The Address-Mr. Desmarais
ture (Mr. Whelan). Noting that the Canadian Prairies are a semi-arid region, the Minister referred to the excess of evaporation over precipitation. He stressed that this condition prevails precisely in those areas where the majority of production for export takes place. "Getting water to the right place at the right moment can make all the difference between success and disaster", says the brief, and I quote:
Let me quote further: "Timing of rainfall can be critical during the growing season. A delay of one or two weeks in rain can make the difference between a bumper crop and crop failure". The Minister adds that the presence of water brings development opportunities which take advantage of positive characteristics of climate, soil and labour availability. Thus a sound irrigation infrastructure, he points out, can provide the basis for strong, diversified economy and employment opportunities.
To give you an idea of the importance of water, it takes
60,000	gallons to produce one tonne of steel and 14,395 gallons to produce a single bushel of wheat. There is a clear and present threat to Canada's ability to sustain productivity in the agricultural sector, and certain areas of the West have already been obliged to call a halt to further industrial development, until adequate water sources can be ensured. These are certainly not the prospects our economy needs at this crucial moment in Canada's history.
Outside of our borders the crisis potential is even clearer. In California and the American southwest, water scarcity is an ongoing and growing concern. Just recently the potential crisis situation has been pointed up in six southwestern states, ranging from west Texas up through the agricultural midwest to Nebraska. And, of course, throughout the U.S. the pollution problem is compounded by its stagnant waterways, inadequate flow and depletion of underground aquifers.
Further south, the arid highlands of northern Mexico stand as a barren monument to the deprived. Other areas of the North American continent which could help feed a hungry world remain unproductive wastelands for lack of adequate irrigation. It is not that there is not enough water to go around. Thanks to its endless renewal in nature's hydrologic cycle there is as much water around today as there was in the time of Julius Caesar.
On the world scene, our constant water supply is estimated at roughly ten times demand and, even allowing for massive population growth, projections still show sufficient over-all global water supplies for the foreseeable future.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the crux of the problem is that this vital resource is not located where it would benefit us most. As far as Canada is concerned, an accident of geography has bestowed on a small fraction of the human race an immense resource, while billions of people are suffering the consequences of poverty and famine. In seventeen years, at the end of this century, the world population will have exceeded the six billion mark. More than five-sixths will be living in developing countries. In that same year 2000, the population of Canada
will be not more than 0.5 per cent of the total population of our global village.
When we consider our rich water resources, the white gold of today, we may well ask ourselves how long we can expect to maintain this privileged position when hunger is everywhere, and mankind is on the brink of a serious crisis. Today, the real challenge is to use our expertise, our technology and our creativity to solve the problem created by the differences between rich and poor. It is clear that water distribution is a matter of life and death for the millions who are starving, and this problem is a very real threat to the survival of our entire civilization. We have the technology to go to the moon. Thanks to our nuclear arsenal we also have the power to wipe out the entire human race. Will future historians be prepared to believe that our intelligence faltered when faced with the problem of water distribution? Today, we must accept the fact that water has become a world resource, and this implies that its distribution must be assured in terms of continental rather than national requirements, if we are to survive until the next century. Canada, however, is hardly in a position to criticize. For over twenty years, we have held the key to world leadership in this area. We could use our water surplus in order to increase the quality of life in Canada and throughout North America. This priceless gift of nature could be used to generate wealth and restore economic stability, without hurting anyone. We shall probably never know what caused us to ignore this path to economic self-sufficiency. Perhaps we needed a shock treatment: the recession with the social disruption of unemployment and economic uncertainty. We are now faced with the realization that the good old days will not come back and that perhaps the time has come . . . The industrial age has come to an end and we are now entering an era where we can no longer count on our non-renewable resources. Our old values are useless. At last we will have to learn to stand on our own two feet.

The practical blueprint to which I referred is the Grand Canal or Grand Recycling and Northern Development Project. This concept is the result of more than one-quarter of a century of dedicated study and effort by one of Canada's leading water management and engineering experts, Thomas W. Kierans of Newfoundland. In essence, the plan involves turning our shallow, shrinking and salty James Bay into a fresh water lake. This would be achieved by building a 100-mile dyke across its junction with Hudson's Bay. This lake would be fed by the run-off from the 750,000 square kilometre surrounding watershed. This run-off totals some 400,000 cubic feet per second or more than one cubic mile of fresh water every three days. All of this precious run-off is now washed uselessly away into the sea.
For the environmentalists, it is worth stressing that this can be achieved without diverting one drop of water from these northern rivers. Each would continue its uninterrupted flow to its normal outlet in James Bay. What is envisaged is simply a
December 12, 1983

recycling as opposed to a diversion of the water supply after it has run its natural course and would otherwise merely be dissipated in the salty vastness of the Arctic Ocean. James Bay, therefore, would become a gigantic reservoir of fresh, pure water to serve the needs of Canada and the continent.
The next stage is the channelling of surplus supplies of pristine, pure water south from James Bay to the Great Lakes. This would be achieved by pumping stations, powered perhaps by nuclear energy, to lift the water to a height of some 900 feet and speed it on its journey to the Canadian heartland. The essence of the plan, however, lies in the central location of the Great Lakes for continent-wide distribution. With their 100,000 square mile area and 580 feet elevation, they constitute a natural reservoir to serve a thirsty North America. One might almost be tempted to think that a benevolent providence had designed the whole thing for our express benefit.
Another godsend is the fact that the distribution can make use of an existing network of vein-like rivers and waterways already covering most of North America. Linked by strategically located canals and regional storage reservoirs, these waterways can carry fresh supplies to our water-short western areas for agriculture, industry and human consumption. With a virtual infusion of new life, it can open up infinite horizons for this country's areas of actual and potential water shortage. An enhanced environment due to ability to reduce flood damage is just one of the spin-off benefits.
Beyond our borders the prospects are even more staggering. Imagine the impact of a revitalized mighty Mississippi carrying fresh, pure water south to the continental heartland, to the thirsty American southwest and the arid highlands of northern Mexico; or consider the implications of a link-up with the Missouri River system and waterways. Perhaps the once great Colorado, now just a trickle where it crosses the Mexican border, may again become a torrent of life-sustaining fluid.
Given adequate supplies of fresh, renewable water, the food producing potential of all these areas is enormous. Combined with Canada's yield and the as yet untapped land of resources of the arid Mexican plains, there is hope for feeding countless millions. And, more immediately, we should think of the results for Canada's economy. Imagine what it would mean to be in a position to export an endlessly renewable, inexhaustible and vital commodity, for which demand can only grow in the future. Consider the wealth to be generated and the jobs to be created.
In addition to the direct creation of new and meaningful jobs for thousands over a very extended period, there are all the implications for northern development. This includes the opening of navigable waterways such as a Great Lakes-Sea-way linking Ontario and Quebec with the eastern Arctic.
With all these increased activities, new employment and long-term sustained increase in our GNP, indeed the future could look very bright indeed for Canadians. All this can be achieved within the context of a vastly enhanced over-all quality of life. Our environment will undergo marked improve-
The Address-Mr. Fennell
ment and we will have pure, palatable water to drink. The opportunity presented to us here is close to incredible. We can use our resources massively to stimulate North American food production without diverting a single drop of our water from its natural course. I repeat, all this can be achieved by recycling; not a drop of water will be diverted.

Of course, all this is not a matter of days or weeks. A project of this kind will need years of planning and hard work, and the sooner we get started the better. As things are today, we have no time to lose. Considering the problems facing North America, there is no doubt that a project of this kind must be developed. It is only a matter of deciding who is going to take the initiative. Considering the magnitude of the costs involved, we will need co-operation on an international scale, as well as the support of various levels of government in Canada.

In conclusion, in Canada's case the most obvious benefits deriving from the Grand Canal project include the following: sustained generation of wealth with an increase in the GNP surpassing the value of all our present wheat production; creation of a wide range of meaningful jobs for Canadians from the project itself and from spin-off developments; opening of vast new areas of North America to produce food to feed a hungry world on the eve of entry into the 21st century; vastly improved prospects for Canada's agricultural and industrial future, bringing fresh life to water-short areas; opening of wide, new horizons of northern development projects including a Great Lakes-Seaway link with the eastern Arctic; introduction of vastly more efficient flood control, water flow and level stabilization throughout Canada's waterways; pollution abatement and provision of pure, fresh drinking water all across the country through flushing out stagnant waterways; development of new fisheries and an over-all enhancement of the Canadian environment from the Arctic to the United States border; stimulation of domestic expertise in a host of areas, including hydraulic engineering, tunnelling techniques, nuclear power, et cetera; and, finally, creation of a new sense of unity and purpose for all Canadians, with pride in the ability to stand on our own economic feet. Within our grasp today lies the ability to achieve all this. Just what, then, are we waiting for?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Are there Hon. Members who wish to ask questions of the Hon. Member for Dollard (Mr. Desmarais) who has just spoken? Since there are none, the Chair will recognize the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell).

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the Hon. Member for Dollard (Mr. Desmarais) on his thoughtful concept for Canada. It sounds very worth the while, but I believe that now is the time to allow the private sector to access the funds and stop government spending. We require the government sector to take advantage of the natural resources of the country. Once the private sector is working and the machinery is in place to generate the revenue, we in

December 12, 1983
The Address-Mr. Fennell
turn can consider his concept. I believe it is very worth while, but it would be taking too much money out of the private sector.
I listened with interest to the Throne Speech, more particularly when 1 consider those who read it. I believe the person who read it would have agreed philosophically with the speech. We must consider that he was the ex-Premier of an NDP government in a province of Canada. It is rather appropriate that he should be the one who spoke at that time.
Also I point out that the entire Throne Speech is another example of the Liberal Government making promises, bringing out new programs, but never finishing anything it starts. I recall vividly-and it was brought to my attention last weekend-when Bruce Phillips read on CTV a paragraph from the previous Throne Speech which in essence indicated that the Government would never allow the increase in gasoline to go to 18 cents. Canadians will recall that. They are well aware that whatever was said this week has little or no meaning in fact. It is just another example of many broken promises.
I would like to commend the author of the Throne Speech, whoever wrote it, because he has made it so much easier for us to run in the next election. I found pitfalls throughout the whole document. There are no facts, absolutely none. It is a great idea without any plan to follow. Having been here four and a half years, I know we have not accomplished 10 per cent of what was promised in the Throne Speech. However, I want to address specifically the lack of initiative and incentive for the industrial sector of Canada. We in Canada have been operating with an interventionist, socialist policy. There are no specific incentives in the Throne Speech for industry. The private sector is tired of change. It needs consistency, something it can live with day in and day out. The private sector cannot exist with tax changes in the system every year. It cannot plan for the next year. In addition, we have fallen far behind in productivity because there has not been consistency in policy.
All that comes out of the Throne Speech is conflict with the private sector and interventionism. Thinking that the Government is better able to pick winners and losers is false. The sooner we get away from that, the better it will be. An interesting comment in the Throne Speech is that for the small business sector, that sector which employs 66 per cent of Canadians, there will be a "buy-Canadian" program developed. Two weeks before the Throne Speech, a Minister who sits in the other place said that Canadians must start buying Russian products. There is a total conflict between the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his ministers.
One program being brought forward is a rehash, other than $269 million of new money. As the Hon. Member for Pro-vencher (Mr. Epp) mentioned, they seem to have these $200 million photo opportunities from time to time and there is another one in the Throne Speech.
The $1 billion youth program is commendable, but only if you depend on partial or band-aid solutions. It does not solve
the problem for the youth of this country and does not create long-term jobs for them. It will provide the youth with some skills and experience, but after six months there will not be one job for those people. They will have to return to unemployment insurance.
We must develop long-term programs for our youth. The only people who can do that are those in the private sector. We have a bureaucracy that creates jobs according to Parkinson's law, but that is not productive. The Government is unaware that we have machinery to get in place. The faster, more effectively and efficiently that machinery operates, the sooner this country will be able to afford the social programs now in place. We require total industrial renewal, stimulation of research and development and higher productivity. We are probably the only country in the world whose productivity has dropped by 4 per cent since the last election.
While every other country has moved ahead, Canada has fallen behind. That is because we are too concerned about esoteric issues rather than paying attention to economic issues. Until we get our industry operating efficiently and creating wealth, we will not have job creation. There is nothing positive in the entire Throne Speech to assist the private sector in creating jobs and thereby wealth which will in turn create additional jobs.
The Throne Speech touches on trading corporations, for international trade. That is extremely commendable. However, unless we deal with productivity, the trading corporations will not have anything to sell. We must identify trading corporations. Certain industries have survived the depression, and I call it a depression because it has gone beyond a recession. In addition to developing trading corporations, we must develop higher productivity.
Part of the problem is that the Government has only increased research and development expenditure from 1.2 per cent to 1.3 per cent of GNP. In the same period, Japan increased its research and development expenditure from 1.83 per cent to 2.23 per cent. 1 should point out that the Government of Japan contributes far less to research and development than the private sector. Interventionist policies for research and development have not worked in Canada. The private sector has the initiative to develop new products and better ways of producing them. Recognition of that is totally lacking in the Throne Speech.
We then get into the wonderful, generalized discussion of the world product mandate. As we know, that deals with multinationals to a great extent. If the tax incentive is there, the multinationals will take advantage of wherever the incentives is greatest. This has been proven internationally for many years.
A prime example of a very successful Canadian multinational is Northern Telecom. It does not want grants and aid. It wants stability. It can then produce a world product. When it moved to the United States three or four years ago, there was severe criticism about its heavy investment there. It had to get out of Canada and go where there was stability to develop
December 12, 1983

world products. Those who criticized Northern Telecom at that time now have to eat their words.
The Throne Speech refers to the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada. That is a wonderful name but what does it mean? It does not say. Maybe it says that we will be more friendly with the people of the Pacific rim. Elowever, without higher productivity we cannot sell to those people. All we can sell is our natural resources and raw materials, and that does not provide jobs in Canada.
1 would like to see some terms of reference set out for the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada. I would like to know their budget, their goals and how they are going to be accomplished. Perhaps it could be a reverse way of getting back into the economy money that has been taken out for other purposes.
The Throne Speech then refers to U.S.-Canada relations. Who caused the problem? It was a Liberal Government attacking our best trading partners, neighbours and cousins that caused the problem. We all know, and I need not say any more about it, that the National Energy Program has been an absolute disaster for our relations with the United States, let alone a disaster for western Canada, as my friend for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) will confirm. It has led Americans to say that we have one rule for our own oil companies, particularly our Government owned oil company, and another set of rules for everyone else.
I would simply like to relate this point to the early days in Canada before Canadians were aware of the major importance of the oil industry. Who had the courage to come to Canada and develop the oil industry? The pension fund did not do it and Bay Street did not do it. The only place for the oil industry to turn was the United States. The Americans had guts whereas we Canadians did not have the guts to develop our own resources. The Americans developed the industry and then the National Energy Program came along and cut them off at the knees.
Another point that has been very offensive, not only to the United States which is our major trading partner but internationally as well, is FIRA. That set of rules is unrealistic. Canadians will not invest in anything that is not secured or guaranteed. They are very much like the people in the Middle East. They will not take the risk unless its success has been proven. I say that we have a bad relationship with our neighbours. Instead of confrontation we need co-operation with our neigbours, because the more we export to the United States, the more jobs we create in Canada.
The Throne Speech mentions bilateral agreements with the petrochemical industry. The petrochemical industry would not need bilateral agreements if it were given tax breaks on raw material. It is those taxes that are destroying that industry. Recently, Petromont was allowed a $50 million grant. Petromont did not want a $50 million grant, it wanted relief for the taxes that are being paid on the raw materials that are turned into finished products and exported out of the country.
The Address-Mr. Fennell
The textiles and clothing industry is a very important industry in Canada. The Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) has said that we must open our borders to textiles from all over the world. We are talking about 200,000 jobs in Canada. How many small entrepreneurs like Alfred Sung are making clothing in Canada? What protection are we to give them? Many of them will leave the country and let us depend upon imports. We are losing our creativity. I would say that the textile industry, under very adverse conditions, has had to depend too heavily upon tariff barriers. It has not been given the incentive to upgrade its facilities, to increase its productivity and to create new ideas because the Government does nothing for the industrial sector.
As 1 said before, we pick winners and we pick losers. The Government has recently picked the helicopter industry as a winner. We should realize that we are only a small sector of the North American market and we must develop our proportion of the GNP that is to go to the North American market. That does not necessarily mean that we will compete with helicopter manufacturing companies elsewhere. Perhaps we will make the blades and the tires or the tail assemblies, as has been done so successfully by McDonnell Douglas Industries in Toronto. That is one area in which we are really failing.
Higher productivity for the world market is of great importance. Since the present Government came into power in 1968, our percentage of world trade has dropped from 5.7 per cent to 3.8 per cent. That has affected at least one million jobs in Canada. At the same time Japan, a country which produced less than Canada in 1968, now carries on twice the amount of international trade. That is because the Japanese have not been dependent upon natural resources. The only thing they have is human resources. They have used their ingenuity to create new products, new jobs and new wealth in their country.
In 1968, there was a deficit of $3.4 billion for fully manufactured goods in Canada. In 1982, that deficit was $13.4 billion. That tells us a great deal about our industrial sector. Furthermore, if it had not been for the automobile industry and the fact that people in North America are still demanding large cars, that deficit would be far in excess of that amount.
The Throne Speech refers to the Japan-Canada auto pact. When we consider the fact that the Government has turned aside the task force report that it requested and has not accepted the recommendations for a value added requirement, a Japan-Canada auto pact would be a one-way street. We will ship all of our raw materials to Japan and we will in turn buy all of our cars from Japan. Again, Mr. Speaker, exporting raw materials is not a solution to the problem of the million and a half people who are looking for jobs. I would like to preserve the Canada-United States auto pact. It has worked well for Canada. I do not want to see any damage done to that auto pact. However, I would like to know what the Japan-Canada auto pact is all about.
The Speech from the Throne refers to research and development. However, it did not refer to any specific goals, targets or direct incentives. To make such broad statements without anything concrete is only to spout rhetoric.

December 12, 1983
The Address-Mr. Fennell
1 would like to conclude by saying that industry in the country does not want handouts. It wants stability. It wants tax relief where it is fair and equitable. The faster our industries operate, the faster we will be able to pay for the social programs that have been implemented. The only thing I request of the Government is to resign, call an election and let the public decide who can best manage the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two questions to ask the Hon. Member. I heard him talk about the auto pact with Japan but I am not sure whether he viewed it favourably or unfavourably. However, I would like to tell him that the task force report has not been rejected by the Government but is under consideration.
I would first like to ask the Hon. Member where he stands on the task force recommendation that there be a 60 per cent Canadian content regulation for foreign automobiles which are imported into the country. Second, with regard to research and development, does the Hon. Member fail to recognize the initiatives that were put forward in the April budget which have been very favourably received by industry and by people in the R and D community and has led to a substantial increase in attendant R and D for this coming year on top of the big increases that were realized in the last two years? We have seen a substantial increase in R and D. The April budget brought forward new measures to stimulate R and D and to allow passthroughs from the R and D companies directly to investors which, according to the industry, will lead to a major stimulus. Is the Hon. Member saying that in addition to that there should have been other measures specifically mentioned in the Speech from the Throne?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose I could have asked the same questions of the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary as we have worked together fairly closely on the Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs Committee. Referring to the Japanese auto pact, I could not comment on that because the speech simply indicates that a Japan-Canada auto pact will be created. I do not know what the concept is and I do not know what is intended by it. I do not know if it means bilateral trade. There is nothing there that would allow me to make a decision. I will be interested in the matter when the legislation comes up.
As far as the task force report is concerned, as with every task force report there will have to be some modifications made. I must, however, support the thrust of that report. There are weaknesses that have crept in. One is the fact that General Motors is going to have to start importing Toyotas under its portion of the agreement. I do not think that was intended to happen so we will have to watch it.
If Canadians can build some portions of the world car effectively-not necessarily assembly-and if we get 60 per cent of the manufacturing, for bumpers or springs, for instance, that would be a worth-while goal and would create jobs in this country.
1 cannot argue with the Parliamentary Secretary about the R and D measures in the April budget. I think the proposals were excellent but they did not go quite far enough. People do not understand them. They should have been made operative for a period of years because the general public and the industry do not know if they will last for this year or for next year. People want to plan for five years.
I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary would admit that there have been some major changes in policy on the Government side that have confronted industry with a conundrum. He mentioned major increases in research and development over the past two years but, Mr. Speaker, we have only gone from 1.2 per cent to 1.3 per cent. The Japanese have done far better.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I comment on the Speech from the Throne 1 want to add my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. It is a pleasure to stand this early in the second session of this Thirty-Second Parliament to observe what the Government has proposed as its legislative program for the oncoming year. As I watched His Excellency reading the Speech from the Throne, I was moved to see that it covered such a broad spectrum of issues, everything from divorce to drinking drivers, from health care to housing, child care to pensions, small business to foreign trade. On the way it takes in charities, broadcasting, the Security Service and emergency planning.
Well, Mr. Speaker, talk about Orwell's 1984. I realize 1984 is next year, but according to this Government's proposals, all we shall have to do from now on is to get up in the morning and everything else will be taken care of, if the Government has the will and the time to bring these proposals in.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with housing as it is dealt with in the Speech from the Throne and as it has been dealt with by this Government in the past decade. The operative part of the speech is as follows:
The Government recognizes the concerns of home owners and potential home buyers about the uncertainty of future mortgage costs. Legislation and other measures will be proposed to further strengthen confidence in the housing market by giving protection to home owners. The choice of mortgage instru-

December 12, 1983
The Address-Mr. Clarke
ments will be broadened. These measures should increase the accessibility and security of home ownership, provide a greater measure of confidence and stability to the home building industry, and enhance the flexibility of the mortgage market.
That raises a number of very important and interesting questions, Mr. Speaker. How did we get into such an awful state that the Government has to propose measures such as these? It says "the concerns of home owners and potential horn buyers". Of course, potential home buyers are all those tenants who are having difficulty covering their heads, as well as home owners. It says "the uncertainty of future mortgage costs". I wonder which government had what economic policies in effect which led to such high mortgage costs, or even such fluctuating mortgage costs? There is no secret about why mortgage costs fluctuate. It says "to further strengthen confidence in the housing market". It was this Government's policies which destroyed confidence in the housing market. When this Party proposed greater protection for home owners in the last Parliament, it was the Official Opposition, now the Government opposite, that was vehemently opposed to those proposed measures.
The mortgage market used to work quite well on its own, Mr. Speaker, but now long-term money has all but dried up because of the uncertainty of the economic policies of this Government. Of course, people are in difficulty and things are in bad shape right now. I want to make it clear that I am not this Party's housing policy critic, but I have spoken many times over the last seven years on housing issues. As one who has been in the housing business for over 20 years, I have watched developments in the industry that 1 am still involved in and I have seen the effects of this Government's policies.
Twenty years ago mortgage rates had just risen to 7 per cent. Imagine that! I remember looking at a deal that was 7 per cent and we were very disappointed and seriously considered not taking the deal because the mortgage rate had gone from 6.75 per cent to 7 per cent. Twenty years ago the apartment vacancy rate in Vancouver's west end was about 20 per cent. I know because 1 was subsidizing tenants in the new buildings as they came in. No help from the Government in those days. It was not needed and was not asked for. Twenty years ago housing prices in Vancouver were less than one-tenth what they are today. A perfectly good building lot in the best area of Vancouver could be purchased for $15,000, and a Shaughnessy mansion, which might cost $750,000 today, could be had for $50,000.
Having looked back at some of the debates in this House on housing, I am glad to see my colleague from Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) here today because I am going once again to quote something she said when she was the housing critic for this Party. In 1975 I referred to a speech she made in November, eight years ago. In replying to a statement of the then Minister of State for Urban Affairs, Mr. Danson, she expressed the views of this Party when she said that we welcome any Government initiative to stimulate the residential construction industry. I stress, Mr. Speaker, to "stimulate the industry"; not to meddle with it, but to stimulate the construction industry. This was particularly so in view of the fact that
moves taken by the Government in the past 18 months have largely been responsible for the depression experienced by this very important sector of the economy. Well, nothing has changed and I am sure my colleague will agree that nothing whatever has changed.
Several times I have argued in this House that the best thing the federal Government could do for the housing industry and for people who have to have housing, whether they be buyers or renters, is to get out of the housing industry. The industry would take care of itself just as it did for a very long time when housing was a lot more readily available and a lot cheaper.
In March, 1973 I argued that, and 1 quote from Hansard for March 22, 1973:
-federal housing policies, current or proposed, do more harm than good, and that the best thing the federal Government could do to help Canadians with their housing problems would be to leave us alone. Disband the bureaucracy, cut taxes and let us solve our own problems, with the interference of our local or provincial government if we choose, but without federal interference; without federal bureaucrats taking our money from us in taxes and spending it as they want to spend it, rather than as we want to spend it.
I had some allies, even in those days, Mr. Speaker. At that time the Vancouver Province editorialized that our housing difficulties, particularly in the rental field, compose a classic case of problem creation by government. Still true, Mr. Speaker. Nothing has been the same since the Government introduced its changes in true accounting principles in 1971. At that time the Government decided, all on its own, that business losses created by capital cost allowances on rental real estate would no longer be deductible from income from other sources. That was probably the first major blow in driving out the suppliers of rental housing and forcing those entrepreneurial Canadians with money to invest to withdraw their support from the housing industry and go elsewhere to invest their money.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RESCUERS OF CREW OF CARGO VESSEL "UNISOL" WRECKED ON ILE DUPUIS, AT CHANDLER, P.Q.
speechtext: Madam Speaker, unfortunately, tragedies are often used as a pretext in the House to present grievances to the Government and to discredit the work of departmental employees and members of the armed forces. Today, I would like to remind the House that on December 7, thirty to forty-foot waves swept along the Gaspe coast, causing serious damage. The Peruvian freighter Unisol was wrecked on the reefs of lie Dupuis near Chandler. At 8.30 a.m., the Quebec Provincial Police at Chandler informed the Coastguard of the freighter's situation, asking that help be sent immediately to rescue the crew. Two Canadian Forces helicopters were dispatched from the Summerside Canadian Forces Base in Prince Edward Island. The rescue operation took place in extremely difficult circumstances, with fifty-mile-an-hour winds. At 12.30 p.m., the thirty-four crew members and pilot Milton Molloy were on dry land. Today, I wish to pay tribute to the members of the Canadian Forces who took part in this rescue operation, to the Coastguard, members of the Quebec Provincial Police in Chandler and the municipal police who co-ordinated emergency measures to rescue the crew of the Unisol.

APPOINTMENT OF MINISTER OF STATE FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the Speech from the Throne it was announced that the Canadian Government proposes to appoint a Minister of State for Youth some time during this session. This decision has been eagerly awaited and recommended by many groups, and I believe that a special Ministry for Youth will be able to channel all its energies into providing for the well-being of young Canadians. 1 am particularly pleased, since last spring, there was a proposal from the Youth Commission of the Liberal Party to create this kind of ministry, a proposal that received the support of our party's general executive. Early last summer, the Liberal Members for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) and Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) and Senator Jacques Hebert recommended a measure of this kind, which received the full support of the caucus of Liberal Members from Quebec at Lac Delage. I am glad that the Progressive Conservative Party is supporting the project, but as usual, their support has come six months too late. Nevertheless, 1 hope they will also support the other youth measures announced in the Speech from the Throne, including the creation of a national voluntary service to help youth employment, the creation of a bonus system for travelling in Canada and all the other measures applying to young people.
* *
*

Madam Speaker, this country was built by young people. John A. Macdonald was only 15 years old when he articled as a lawyer. J. Wesley Dafoe was only 19 when he became the first editor of the Ottawa Journal. William Van Florne was just 14 when he started his railroad career. Instead of real job creation, the Liberals use Monty Python doublespeak and sleight of hand to delude today's youth.
On April 18 of this year the then Minister of Employment and Immigration announced the youth initiative program with over $1 billion for employment and training. The same program reappears in the Speech from the Throne. This time it is called the Youth Opportunity Fund. Ministers promised us
10,000	jobs in a conservation corps, which now concerts to a new name. Environment 2000. Instead of 10,000 jobs, we now get 4,600. On December 7 the Minister claimed youth job creation at 125,000. The next day he reduced the figure to
90,000.	In one night he spilled 35,000 jobs. This is an attempt to deceive the youth of Canada. There are no new dollars.
This is a Government whose imagination is limited to shortterm employment for 20 per cent of the unemployed youth.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: DEPARTMENT'S DELAY IN ISSUING REFUNDS TO TAXPAYERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is a growing concern among Canadians about the annual delay in processing income tax returns. In 1983, particularly. Revenue Canada had such a backlog of unprocessed income tax returns that some areas refused to accept individual inquiries from taxpayers on when they could expect a refund, indicating, in a recorded message in June, they could expect an additional wait of at least 10 weeks for a refund, despite compliance by the taxpayers with the filing deadline.
Revenue Canada officials have stated continually that the delay in processing tax returns and issuing refunds is caused by Parliament's failure to expedite approval of amendments to the income tax laws. Even though Revenue Canada paid interest at 10 per cent on refunds to those who met the filing deadline, many Canadian taxpayers became so frustrated, or were so financially hard pressed, that they flocked to income tax firms which offered instant refunds at a discount rate, as opposed to waiting further.
It is of concern to me, Madam Speaker, that Canadians arc subjected to this type of inconvenience due to the delays encountered in receiving their tax refunds. 1 therefore urge this House to consider remedies to this problem and recommend particular emphasis be placed on reviewing the propriety of the procedural tactics invoked by the Opposition which contributed substantially to the delay in passage of amendments to the income tax laws.

TRANSIT SERVICE DEFICITS-NEED FOR FEDERAL GOVERNMENT FUNDING
