Madam Speaker, Canadian municipalities require a commitment very soon from the federal Government that there will be a suitable replacement for the Urban Transportation Assistance Program. Under that program many municipalities acquired federal funds for transit related capital projects. This Program expires in March of next year, but for all intents and purposes it is already over. Most of the funds have already been spent, and in my home Province of Manitoba no new projects are being approved.
There is some urgency attached to this matter in that municipalities want to know, before they begin their annual budget deliberations, whether they can count on a program similar to UTAP. Their concern is understandable.
December 12, 1983

It is a fact of life that most municipal transit services operate at a deficit. The smaller ones particularly rely on capital assistance from higher government levels. 1 am convinced that many municipalities will face serious, eleven desperate budgetary problems if the federal Government does not come up with an adequate replacement for UTAP. Therefore I urge the Minister of Transport to recommend to Cabinet a program with a funding arrangement similar to UTAP. In that way the federal Government would continue to offer 80 per cent capital funding for municipal transit projects. Such a program should receive cabinet support as soon as is reasonably possible.

Thank you, Madam Speaker, and welcome back. Last week two young boys appeared before the Macdonald Royal Commission on the Economy and pointed out that for many young Canadians Santa Claus is dead. SOVIET EMBASSY'S ATTACK ON UKRAINIAN CANADIANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, all Canadians of Ukrainian descent were viciously slandered last weekend when an official of the Soviet Embassy referred to the Congress of Free Ukrainians meeting in Toronto as a "gathering of former Nazi lackies and supporters' . Canadians of every ethnic background and race will feel nothing but repugnance and outrage at such an unwarranted and malicious attack.
Oral Questions
During the Second World War untold thousands of Ukrainian Canadians answered their country's call and volunteered to fight against Adolf Hitler and the national socialist policies for which he stood. They served in every facet of the Armed Forces and distinguished themselves in every field of battle. Many gave their lives in the cause. Through his words, the Soviet Embassy spokesman has sought to defile the sacrifices and contributions made by those men and women.
The smear campaign launched against Ukrainian Canadians by the Soviet Union has underlined the Embasy's lack of credibility. This is a country whose Embassy refused to accept delivery of a diplomatic note from the House of Commons after a coldblooded attack on a defenceless Korean KAL airliner. This is a country and a system of government that were directly responsible for the man-made famine that swept the Ukraine in 1932-33, resulting in the deaths of some seven million Ukrainians.
Along with thousands of other Canadians of Ukrainian heritage, 1 am outraged at being termed a "nazi lackey". There can be no excuse for such a scurrilous and abusive attack.
When it comes to a question of totalitarianism versus freedom, it is clear that Ukrainian Canadians stand on the side of liberty, freedom, and justice.

subsubtopic: LACK OF REFERENCE IN SPEECH FROM THRONE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Economic Development. Recently the Minister gave a very thoughtful speech relating the income tax system with productivity. Of the income tax system, he said that it was inequitable, unduly complex, and was not making the contribution that it should to economic growth. With that, Members on this side agree. The tragedy is not only that the Minister understands the problem and knows the solution, but nothing has been done. Why was no priority given to this statement in the Speech from the Throne?

December 12, 1983
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: LACK OF REFERENCE IN SPEECH FROM THRONE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is not true that nothing is being done. As the Hon. Member probably knows, when the Minister of Finance addressed that same body, the Canadian Tax Foundation in 1982, he underlined the problem of complexity which exists in income tax law. Subsequent to that, I understand that a committee was struck between the Canadian Tax Foundation and the Department of Finance. To my knowledge, that committee has not yet reported. There obviously will be progress made on that front, particularly with respect to small business and other such sectors.
In addition, the Hon. Member will know that the Minister of Finance has recently introduced legislation with respect to research and development in order to introduce a new mechanism which allows a flow-through of tax credits, which was raised in the April budget. It was subsequently confirmed as a good idea by the community, the clientele which it affects. That will go a long way toward permitting equity to flow in a less complicated fashion into that particular sector.
I do not think it is fair to say that nothing has been done. Something is being done all the time. As I stated in that speech, complexity still exists in many areas. All of us must constantly try to address the problems of making the Income Tax Act more simple and effective, and make it contribute in that fashion to economic development and growth.

Madam Speaker, in the same speech the Minister said: "I blame the complexities and the burdens of our tax system that drive taxpayers to seek tax savings as an end unto themselves rather than putting talent and capital to other productive and profitable purposes." That is the problem with the economy. As the senior Minister in terms of economic development, why was no priority given in the Speech from the Throne to this threshold question?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the issue of taxation and making the tax system, making it effective, making it simple, and making it contribute to economic growth, is a continuing priority of the Government. It is not a new initiative that had to be introduced in the Speech from the Throne. The point I make with respect to seeking tax savings for their own sake is one which has bothered me for many years as a tax practitioner. I am sure that all Members of this House will agree. It is a problem with which we have wrestled, and with which the United States and other jurisdictions have wrestled. Surely the massive brain power which we have wandering around in the Income Tax Act could be put to better use elsewhere, particularly in the laboratories of this country.

Mr. Speaker, before 1 was interrupted for the lunch break I was explaining the comments which appeared in the Vancouver newspaper The Province some eight years ago concerning the state of the housing industry, and comments which appeared in The Globe and Mail in 1975. The paragraph that I referred to recently said that rents, like other prices, go up, and that there is no magic umbrella to shelter property owners from inflation. It asked, if mill rates rise, fuel rates rise, if the cost of materials, appliances, mortgages, hydro, water and wages all rise, how can the rent that is made up of all these things stay the same? The writer of the article then asked how long the activists, or indeed the tenants themselves, would sit still for control on their own wages and salaries. The voters gave their answer to that in the 1974 election when they rejected wage and price controls, only to have them imposed by the Government 15 months later.
The Government's chief housing instrument, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, has grown over the years into an enormously complicated corporation. If I may, I will refer Your Honour to the December 31, 1982 issue of the public accounts of Canada which shows the total assets of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to be over $10 billion and its borrowings from the Government of Canada to be over $10 billion also. In other words, this is just a shell corporation by which the Government takes money from one set of taxpayers and lends it to another set of taxpayers. The question is, to whom should these moneys be loaned and how is it decided to whom they should be loaned? If it were a matter of good management, one might be more sympathetic to the aims of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I should like to read Note 2 of the audited financial statement of December 31, 1982, concerning real estate. It shows that the over-all appraised value of real estate is in excess of its book value by $17 million. However, potential losses on specific properties could amount to $28 million, according to the report, based on appraised values determined at November 30, 1982. Later in the report an item appears under the heading "General Administration" which shows real estate operating losses of $6.6 million and real estate disposal losses of $15.5 million. That is all part of a total of $1.6 billion shown in the statement under the heading "Total Charge to the Government of Canada". In other words, that $1.6 billion, including those losses, is not even in the corporate accounts of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
One might ask why that is important. A recent report issued by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation showed that very many middle income Canadians were benefiting from the programs it offered in subsidized housing. Canadians earning $30,000, $40,000 or $50,000 per year were found to be living in subsidized units. The same study showed that some officials in Vancouver were found to be living in Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation units, although I think they have since been moved out. That shows the kind of abuse that can develop with an instrument like Canada Mortgage and Housing Cor-

December I 2, 1983
The Address-Mr. Clarke
poration running away with billions of taxpayers' dollars, not knowing what to do with them or to whom to give them.
In 1978, 1 was a member for an all-Party task force of the House which went to the United States to study the experience there and proposed legislation to deal with mortgage interest and property tax deductibility. They have some instruments which have run amok and if we go this route, we will be in the same position very soon. I refer to the instruments known as "Ginny Mae" and "Fanny Mae"-the General National Mortgage Assistance Program and the Federal National Mortgage Assistance Program. They all come under this huge bureaucracy called Housing and Urban Development, or HUD as it is known in the U.S. It is in the business of providing housing units. They have developed a huge bureaucracy to construct, operate and maintain their housing units. The result has been that the subsidized housing units are better than those the taxpayers who are paying for the subsidized housing can afford. In other words, the equation has gone backwards and those who arc paying cannot afford the housing they are providing for those who supposedly cannot afford it.
In its portfolio, Mr. Speaker, Canada Mortgage and Housing has other examples of the ineptitude and bad management practices that I am afraid we are going to see more and more of. I refer specifically to a development in Vancouver called Granville Island, which some in Vancouver call "Basford's boondoggle" because he was the Minister of Urban Affairs at that time and Granville Island is located in his former riding of Vancouver Centre. At that time I was critical of CMHC taking over the Granville Island development, a light industrial area, to become a retail and artsy section of town. It is a very popular place, no question about that, but it has nothing whatever to do with mortgages or housing. What was the result? Well, through CMHC the taxpayer provided subsidized rents for selected merchants who managed to get into Granville Island and therefore unfairly compete with merchants in commercially provided space. The battle was on. The Government found the administration of this development to be a convenient place to put former Liberal Party supporters.
It has now come full circle, Mr. Speaker, because recently I was visited in my constituency office by a group of merchant tenants. They are having great difficulty with CMHC, which is using totally unprofessional and unbusinesslike methods in running this place so that it is going to be a disaster very soon. Certain tenants are being put out of their space for no reason. Their lease expires and they want to renew but cannot find out what the new rents are except that they are higher than the rents under private sector owners. That is what we are going to have if we do not have a better idea about what this Government wants to do in a critical area like housing which affects absolutely every Canadian.
I have heard a lot recently from the other side about the policies on this side, whether we have any or whether they are any good. Since the opening of this session of Parliament I was able to distribute a very long list of statements made by this
side about various policies. I would like to remind the House, especially Members opposite, that the policies of this Party, developed over many decades and which were in place on June 10, 1983, did not all of a sudden change on June 11 just because we had a leadership convention and elected a new Leader. The policies of this Party on various subjects are well known in basic terms, and as has been pointed out by the Leader and various other members of this Party, details will have to wait until the Government screws up its courage and gets around to calling an election. We have seen the statements by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) about medicare, but it took until today for the Government to table a Bill which will tell us in detail what its policies are, at which time we will be able to respond.
Earlier this year we saw the former Minister of Transport fly his trial balloon or kite over the Crow rate policy. Then the Government wanted to know what our attitude was. Fortunately we waited because the big Liberal caucus in Quebec got to the Minister, and when the time came the Government introduced a Bill on the Crow rate which was totally different from the issues first put forward.
I see my time has expired, Mr. Speaker, and I thank you very much.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising in the House today, because Friday was a particularly interesting day in the House of Commons.

Last Friday was a great day because it was in fact the first speech on policy from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. December 12, 1983

Mulroney), and we had a masterful speech by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau). It was amazing to compare the two. Of course, when we hear the people from the other side of the House, they all complain that our Prime Minister is not effective, that the Party is short of ideas and so on. So the contrast this week, Mr. Speaker, is very fabulous.
On Friday the Prime Minister made a speech that was so good that even Charles Lynch had to say that it was very, very good. He said it was the best speech he ever heard in the House from the Prime Minister. He said that Brian Mulroney, even if he were to be here 20 years, would never achieve such a level of contribution to the House of Commons.
When we look at the substance of the Speech from the Throne, most observers say there is too much in it. That is probably the first time in my life that I hear something like that. People have said it is not a program for the last session of Parliament, but a program for the complete Parliament.
The people who say we are running out steam will now have to recognize two things: the Leader of my Party made a speech that put the Leader of the Opposition in the league he belongs, the midget league; and that we have produced a Throne Speech with so much that most policy observers say we could not implement any part of it because there is not enough time. But what is good for members of my Party is that we have been able to prove in the last few days that, despite all the rumours, there is a lot of energy and vigour on this side of the House.
When we compare that with the performance of the Leader of the Opposition, who was more or less making his maiden speech in the House of Commons, it gave us a lot of satisfaction and hope. Looking at the Leader of the Opposition we thought that maybe after six months he might come up with something; that would have been normal. Of course, he is a very brave man. He has not held one press conference since he became the Leader of the Opposition. We understand that the man might be nervous, but we thought that with all the time he had. two days having passed since the Speech from the Throne was read, the Leader of the Opposition would come up with something. We were hoping that the kid from Baie Comeau would produce something very substantial. But what did we hear on policy? Absolutely nothing.
The only thing they are able to talk about on the other side is a few principles which they talk of all the time. First they claim that the deficit is too big and we should cut taxes. We listen to the Leader of the Opposition and the members of the Opposition these days saying that the problem with medicare is that we should put money into it. They complain that at this time we are planning to increase the supplement which we pay to the old age pensioners in Canada. I am happy to have the opportunity to give the Leader of the Opposition some clarification because he is somewhat confused about the policy. When referring to the back-in, the Leader of the Opposition stated "... to break your word and confiscate someone else's property". Perhaps I can take a couple of minutes to explain this. This is not well understood in Canada and even less so by the Opposition.
When I was the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in 1970, we had a system in Canada lands that we called the checkerboard. We were giving a square to an industry-let's say a square mile-to drill. If a company discovered some oil, it had to revert half of its lands to the Crown without compensation. That was the system.
In theory, if the square mile was full of oil, the company would be obliged at that time to return half of the oil to the Crown free of charge. That was the regime at that time, and the industry did not like it. It asked me for a new regime. I repealed the order and we began negotiations in 1970.
At the end of the negotiations ten years later we have a new regime whereby we take back 25 per cent and we pay for the cost of the find. Previously we did not pay anything. The Americans got excited about this and claimed that it was confiscation after the fact. Let me tell you that before 1970 we were taking back half of the lands. If there was oil, we were taking half of it. But now we are taking 25 per cent and we are paying for that. Where the argument by the Opposition, the Americans and the oil companies is false is that between 1970 and 1980 nobody knew what the regime was to be. I repealed the regime in 1970. When they were sinking pipe in the ground they did not know what the regime was to be between 1970 and 1980. Companies just gambled. They knew a new regime was to come. If they were imprudent between 1970 and 1980, why blame the Government? When the opposition members call this confiscation, let me tell them that Mr. Peckford in Newfoundland thinks that 25 per cent confiscation is not enough, that we should confiscate 40 per cent. Your friend and my friend. Premier Buchanan, is quite ready to accept 25 per cent confiscation right away.
I wanted to have a little more time, Mr. Speaker, to explain that aspect. 1 keep saying, when I meet representatives of the industry who complain now, that they would have been well advised to agree with me in 1970 and not wait until 1980 for the new regime. They gambled and they lost. I do not think at all that the regime means confiscation. It is a law of Parliament which has replaced another law. In the meantime, no one knew what that regime was to be. They gambled.
I went to Norway last summer and I am telling you, Mr. Speaker, that the regime we have in Canada is nothing compared to what they have to take on the nose or on the chin, or whatever it is called in Norway. What the industry wants is one thing. It is stability. That is what we have given to the industry. Now the industry knows what it has got. Things are working. There is much less controversy about this policy now. We have signed agreements with the provinces. What the industry wants most is to tear off the name of the game, to live by rules, and the industry will be happy. That is exactly why I do not want to change things now. I want to give stability to the industry.

The point is that either you proceed by way of grants or through tax incentives. For the same level of activity, it costs the Government, exactly the same amount of money. One way you give grants and you take money out of the Treasury to pay for them. When you have tax incentives, the people who normally pay tax do not pay tax, so you do not get revenue into the Treasury. For the same amount of activity, it costs the Treasury the same. However, the mechanisms arc different. When you give a grant, you can favour one company over another. We did things deliberately in this program because we wanted to help Canadians participate in the Canadian oil and gas industry. If we had proceeded as we proceeded before, through tax incentives, the cost to the Treasury would have been the same but the only companies to benefit from the program would have been the multinationals, as the situation was prior to the National Energy Program. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly welcome this rather rare opportunity to participate in a debate on the Speech from the Throne. As we all know, it has been a long time since the last one. After waiting some 3.5 years, I found it somewhat ironic that last Wednesday, a typical Canadian December day, the Ottawa airport was closed, preventing many Hon. Members of the House, including myself, from hearing the Throne Speech. As 1 learned later with a great deal of disappointment-but I must say without much surprise after having an opportunity to read it-1 did not miss very much.
If I have learned nothing else in the last four and a half years I have been in the House, I have learned that one should not hold one's breath waiting for a Liberal Government, or a Tory Government for that matter, to do anything meaningful, innovative or sincere in addressing the myriad problems facing Canadian society and indeed the world society today.
The Throne Speech addressed three major themes-jobs, medicare and peace. As well it should have; no one can argue that these are not the three most important concerns of our society today. However, one can certainly quarrel with the Government's proposed solution's to these concerns. In the area of jobs, with over 1.5 million Canadians out of work, with a half million of them being young people, the Government is offering something like $300 million in short-term band-aid solutions. That $300 million is like spitting in the Pacific Ocean.
In the area of medicare, which has been under increasing pressure for the past few years, we have learned this afternoon that there will finally be some action, the Canada Health Act having been tabled today. The Minister has been promising the House this Canada Health Act for well over a year and a half. If the Government and if the Minister are really sincere in their oft expressed concern or commitment to preserve medicare, why did they wait so long to take any action?
In the area of peace, the promises in the Speech from the Throne offered less real initiatives than those offered in 1980. Given that the promises made in 1980 were for the most part either abandoned or greatly weakened, one might be forgiven for being somewhat sceptical about the success of current peace initiatives. Supportive? Yes, we are. We are very supportive of these initiatives but, alas, we are not terribly hopeful that the Government will deliver on them.
in the few minutes available to me this afternoon I want to address in particular two topics. The first is what the Throne Speech will do for my constituency of Selkirk-Interlake or, more specifically, what it will not do. Second, I want to comment somewhat on the peace initiatives. In preparing to make my comments today, I reread my speech of April 1980 in reply to that year's Throne Speech. I was struck by how little had changed. On looking over that speech, I discovered that I could have reread most of it today and those comments would have been appropriate in reply to this year's Throne Speech. I was also struck by the article of a regular columnist who covers the Hill which pointed out that not very much had changed from this Throne Speech to the one of 1978.
December 12, 1983

In April, 1980 1 said that my constituents share with most Canadians a desire to share in the good life that we know the country can offer. They share the same frustrations at not being able to share fully in this good life. They share the hardships, both economic and social, that are the results of decades of unconcerned and misdirected government in our country. In that 1980 speech, 1 spoke of the farmers, their problems and concerns, one of which at that time was their fear that sooner or later they were going to lose the benefits of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates. As we all know, that has now gone. Almost immediately, instead of getting the great benefits which the Government promised us, farmers are already feeling the adverse effects of that change.
This last week I received a letter from a farmer in my constituency in the Town of Stonewall. He wrote that the Canadian Wheat Board will not be introducing regular quota increases until after January I, when the new rates take effect. It does not take much to figure out that Canadian National and Canadian Pacific are once again putting it to the farmers. They are refusing to move grain until such time as they will be getting paid more for that movement. This is known to my friends to the right as corporate fair play. Let me read a paragraph from that letter which my constituent Mr. Ross wrote to me:
This is distressing to me and many other farmers. We are operating in a period of depressed grain prices and high production costs. Year-end is a time when many bills must be paid including crop insurance, taxes, mortgages, et cetera. A cash flow is necessary to meet these obligations, and we depend on an increased quota at this time of the year. Moreover, considerable difficulty is experienced by many farmers in reaching granaries and loading grain during mid-winter.
As a layman in the field of agriculture, I have always been mystified by the fact that the return that a farmer receives for his work does not at all reflect the increases in his costs. This has not changed for years, let alone since 1980. This is a problem that is getting very close to the breaking point. It must be addressed and solved very soon, or we will have catastrophic effects both for the Canadian farmers and the many people around the world whom we feed, yet we see nothing in the Throne Speech to address those specific concerns.
In my 1980 speech, I spoke as well of the concerns of the fishing industry, a very important sector in my constituency. I will at this point recognize the one positive item in the Throne Speech that I have come across, that is the increase in the fishing vessel assistance program. Aside from that, continuing low prices, and in some cases even decreased prices, for fish, along with the continuing stagnant economy, have made the fishing industry in Manitoba less viable today than it was in 1980. As well, the ongoing construction of the Garrison Diversion unit in North Dakota of which I have spoken often in this House, continues to pose further threats to the viability of this industry.
In 1980, I also spoke of the plight of my constituents who are natives. 1 said at that time that the natives of Selkirk-
The Address-Mr. Sargeant
Interlake were concerned about unemployment, the lack of adequate educational opportunity and the lack of decent housing. They are disturbed about the lack of understanding among the bureaucrats in the Department of Indian Affairs. They asked to be allowed to run their own lives, a not unreasonable request in Canada of the 1980s.
Very recently a report on Indian self-government was tabled in the House. It was a remarkable report, not only for its contents, which are bold, far-reaching and would go a long way toward addressing and eventually solving many of the concerns of Canadian Indians, but also remarkable for the process by which it was produced. Members of all Parties of this House, each with their own political interests and political biases, worked together with representatives of the Canadian Indians to reach this agreement.
It is no secret that Canadian Indians for very obvious reasons have come to distrust the white governments of this land. They have waited for over 200 years in this part of the country and for over 100 years in my part to be treated with the minimum of rspect deserving to human beings, but especially to Canada's first peoples. One group of Indian bands in my constituency has become so distrustful of the Ottawa Government that they do not believe in the good intentions of this report on self-government. They fear that it is simply a means of taking more power away from the Indians. Let me quote from an article in a recent edition of the Winnipeg Sun. quoting Chief Bill Traverse of the Jackhead Reserve in my constituency. It reads:
The new law is such that the Indian nations will be told how to run their governments and they'll be forced to deal with several departments, which only multiplies the troubles they now have with one Department of Indian Affairs.
I do not share Chief Traverse's concern at this time. Having played a very small part in the preparation of that report, I believe in the sincerity of its framers. I believe it will have very positive benefits for our natives if and when it is implemented.
The Government promised in the Throne Speech to implement that report. I say to the Government today that this is one time that it must live up to its promise to Canada's Indians. Indeed, it is absolutely imperative that we not let the Indians down yet again.
This Throne Speech does little for my constituents. It gives them very little hope that their lot is to improve in either the immediate or long-term future. Certainly we welcome the crumbs that will come from the few extra dollars available for Canada Works and other such programs. In these difficult times, we would be fools to reject even these small amounts. However, we want real jobs, real opportunities to live a full and decent life that we know our country is capable of providing to all Canadians, if only we had the governments with the guts to lead us in the directions necessary to provide those opportunities.
I would like to comment for a few moments on the peace initiative mentioned in this Throne Speech. We in this corner of the House certainly welcome the priority given by the Throne Speech to the pursuit of peace as a paramount goal of Canada and Canadians. As I said a few moments ago in this

December 12, 1983
The Address-Mr. Sargeant
speech and on numerous other occasions over the past few weeks, 1 and my Party are fully supportive of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his current mission to assist in breaking the logjam that is the present state of the arms reduction talks between the superpowers.
Most Canadians of all political stripes support the Prime Minister, with the possible exception of a few members of the Tory caucus who this morning heckled the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) when he was detailing some of the fears that many of us share about nuclear war. God knows that we in this Party have long called for the Canadian Government to play such an intermediary role.
While we support the Prime Minister's intentions, we have some serious problems with his actions. In the course of his current mission, the Prime Minister has used such words as "new, bold and innovative" among others, to describe what is needed to unblock the arms talks, yet this Throne Speech offers nothing that is new, bold or innovative. Indeed, it is a step back from what was contained in the 1980 Throne Speech. If I have time later, I will elaborate on that. The message I want to get to the Prime Minister today, a message that this Party has been trying to get him to understand for quite some time, is that he cannot work both sides of the street. On Friday the Prime Minister chided the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) for being so unwilling to taka a stand that he even tried to take both sides in the recent Grey Cup game. The Prime Minister should listen to his own words. If the Prime Minister is sincere in his stated desire to "create the conditions for greater security and lower levels of armament", as was stated in the Throne Speech, then he must change his Government's policy. If he wants to be taken seriously in his role as intermediary, not only by the world at large but particularly by the leaders of the two superpowers, without whose co-operation he cannot even begin to have success, then he cannot be slavishly tied to the foreign policy of one of those superpowers. Just think for a moment how receptive NATO would be to a peace initiative led by Czechoslovakia or East Germany, for instance. If the Prime Minister wants to be taken seriously in his stated desire to "slow the steady spiral of the arms race, halt the spread of nuclear weapons", then how can he allow his Government to continue to co-operate in that arms race?
Let me give you three examples of that co-operation, Mr. Speaker. The first and most obvious example is the Cruise missile. The development of this missile clearly violates one of the specific points in the Prime Minister's own strategy of suffocation, which was first enunciated at the 1978 special session on disarmament at the United Nations and reaffirmed in the 1980 Throne Speech. That specific point called for a stop to the flight testing of any new delivery system. It seems odd that the Government is pledging in the Throne Speech to expand resources for research and development on verification while at the same time it is aiding to develop a missile that is supposed to render verification meaningless.
The second example of this co-operation, Mr. Speaker, is the MX missile, a much more accurate ICBM than the current arsenal of Minuteman missiles. We know that Boeing of Canada and Bristol Aerospace, both situated in Winnipeg, have been doing R and D work for well over a year now on the MX re-entry vehicle system. We also know that the federal Government, through DIPP, has made an initial commitment to fund Boeing's bid for a production in the development of the Cruise missile guidance system to the tune of $48 million, the Government is directly contributing to a less stable international environment.
As well, Mr. Speaker, there is a third example of this co-operation. I have learned that the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources has been doing extremely accurate mapping of the earth's gravitational field in the Arctic. This information is passed on to the Department of National Defence which, 1 am told, passes it on to the United States to help increase the accuracy of its ICBMs.
It is all well and good for the Government to say that Canadian forces will not be armed with nuclear weapons, but these three examples show that its hands are dirty. It contributes to the growing instability and threat of nuclear war. The Government does not actually need to deploy the weapons to contribute to the instability which new generations of nuclear weapons bring to the international scene. An important and obvious point to be made is that by helping the United States develop its counterforce arsenal, we are only encouraging the Soviets to develop their own counterforce weapons systems. Let me repeat, Mr. Speaker, that if the Prime Minister really wants to be effective in his mission, a mission in which we all desperately want him to succeed, and if the Prime Minister wants the continued support of all Canadians and all world citizens, then he must remove these contradictions.
Let me conclude by saying that I am worried for my country. I am worried because we are getting nothing meaningful from the tired, cynical and discredited Liberal Government. I am worried because we get nothing from the Tory Opposition. We get no definite alternatives except for a few simplistic Reaganite policies, which three and four years ago proved to be failures in both the United Kingdom and the United States and were rightfully abandoned. Canada needs a commitment to provide a decent quality of life to each and every Canadian through peace on the international scene and security at home. Sadly, neither the Government nor the Opposition offers this.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in reply to the Speech from the Throne. Canadians for the most part are probably unaware that we have just started the second session of the Thirty-second Parliament and that on November 30, 1983, we closed the first session of the Thirty-second Parliament, which began

December 12, 1983
in April, 1980 and was the longest session of Parliament in Canadian history. It was an historic session because in those three and a half years, we have seen a world recession that took many Canadians by surprise. No one Canadian, 1 am sure, could have predicted at the beginning of 1980 how deep that recession would be. During that session, Parliament was presented with 200 Bills and it passed 150 pieces of legislation.
I might say that during that session, some great legislation was passed, beginning with the Constitution for Canada. The Canada Act brought the British North America Act to Canada with an amending formula, which may not be perfect but which allows Canadians to amend their Constitution. The Constitution also incorporates a Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which will have an effect on Canadians for many years because Governments, both federal and provincial, as well as individuals and businesses, can now be challenged for violations of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
During the past session, we also implemented the National Energy Program. With this major government initiative, Canada should achieve energy self-sufficiency by 1990. Major oil and gas explorations are presently taking place on the East Coast because of this program. This economic activity has been good for Nova Scotia and 1 hope, with proper direction from industry and Governments, that program will continue to be developed and will bring a new prosperity to the East Coast.
Along with these two major endeavours of the Government, the six and five program was introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) a year and a half ago. Canadians rose to the challenge of reducing inflation in Canada, and today the level of inflation is at 4.9 per cent. During this same period of time, Canada has seen its export trade increase. The Crow rate was reformed to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain. We on the East Coast in particular hope to see a continuation of the expansion of the fishing industry. 1 will return to that matter in a few moments.
Canadians everywhere are concerned with existing world tensions. I recently attended a school poster competition in one of the areas which I represent. The children in the elementary grades had been asked to draw posters indicating what peace in the world meant to them. Children reflect what adults feel. All of those posters reflected the need for peace.
1 am glad that the Speech from the Throne addresses the direction that this Government will take toward global peace, and 1 am pleased that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has launched Canada, through his personal initiatives, toward a goal of restoring the political will necessary for serious dialogue between the East and West on nuclear disarmament. As the Speech from the Throne so clearly states, Canadians need to continue to look for a global partnership for peace in order to ensure a national partnership for prosperity. We can only have that prosperity if the world is also working toward prosperity in a peaceful way.
The Speech from the Throne has been called an action program. It has been called a program which seeks to consolidate the gains of the past three years; a program to reduce inflation; to develop a new and more modern competitive
The Address-Miss Campbell
industrial base; to train the labour force for future jobs; to maintain the social safety net; and to protect and extend the rights of Canadians.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, this debate also allows an opportunity for Members of Parliament to talk about the concerns which exist in their constituencies. My constituency. South West Nova, is in the southwestern end of Nova Scotia, and like many constituencies across Canada, it is a rural area. The largest town in the area, Yarmouth, is approximately
8,000	people. Yarmouth is a gateway to the United States for Canadians, and a gateway for Americans to visit Canada. The area has many years of experience in dealing with Americans. Early in our history the southern end of Nova Scotia carried on a great sailing trade with the Boston states. Today we maintain a ferry which goes between Nova Scotia and Maine year round, and during the summer a second ferry goes between the two areas. South West Nova is very dependent on the sea, but not only for trade, as we also have a good fishing industry.
1 have concerns about the over-all direction of the fishery on the East Coast. What assurances do we have that the two new companies will operate more efficiently than the old companies? My first concern, after the restructuring Bill, is the additional guarantees of more quotas to the fleets of these two companies. Mr. Speaker, these companies had tremendous supplies of fish in the past and will continue to have that supply; yet they could not market this supply efficiently. Why give them additional quotas to make them viable? Why not see if the operations can be managed properly with the supply they presently have?
The Kirby Task Force was a mistake in my view, because we had to wait two years for the solution and the solution should have been attended to two years ago. The Governments-and I add an "s" because provincial Governments are involved-should have helped those plants which could be efficient; they should have formed new ideas for the excesses Dr. Kirby talks about which existed either within the fishing industry or elsewhere; they should have separated the offshore fleet from the companies and have allowed the fleet to stay within its share of the total allowable catch but let it fish to onshore capacity. This would provide for better distribution of the resource both in terms of catching and in terms of marketing.
If this had been done two years ago, there would not be the problems of additional quotas for the two super-companies. Extra redfish in the Gulf and northern cod could be auctioned by this fleet throughout the Atlantic provinces to the processing plants.
The Nova Scotia inshore fishermen who have been able to market all their catch will not be protected by either Government in the new agreement between Nova Scotia and the federal Government. There will be no assurances written into the agreement for the inshore plants' supply of fish. In fact, the independents and fishermen who have survived the last two

December 12, 1983
The Address-Miss Campbell
years will not get additional increases in fish quotas, but the two new supercompanies will. They will be guaranteed access to the quotas for five years. My concerns arc real Mr. Speaker. Where will the fishing industry be in five years? Will the federal Government and the Provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland still be required to deal with the problems of the offshore groundfish industry? I may be pessimistic, Mr. Speaker, but my concerns reflect those of my constituents and other areas of the East Coast.
South West Nova is also a very good farming area. We have good dairy farmers, some beef farming and fruit farms. We have some of the best mink producers in Canada. We have an active hog industry, and we also have a very real involvement with forestry. The area has been protected to some extent from the recession because our local industry is based on primary resources and we have been able to sell our goods. However, Mr. Speaker, all these industries are seasonal and we are forever looking to acquire longer attachment to the work force for the people who make their homes in South West Nova. Because of the seasonality of employment we are perhaps an area, like many other areas in rural Canada, heavily involved in the unemployment insurance system and the need for job creation. I welcome the additional funding for employment programs, particularly the programs directed toward youth, which we heard about in the Speech from the Throne.
I should like to mention one employment program introduced this past summer by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts), which I think will be very beneficial for the people of Nova Scotia and, in particular. South West Nova. That is the Local Employment Assistance and Development Program better known as LEAD. It begins on April 1, 1984, and it is designed to respond to persistent local unemployment and economic problems that are communitywide in scope. The objective is to increase the number of permanent jobs by enabling community representative organizations to plan and carry out employment development activities that relate directly to the community's own objectives. Eligible communities include those with a population of less than 50,000 which would meet the following criteria: have an employment problem which is persistent and more serious than in the general area; have potential for increased employment; and have demonstrated a capacity for planning an economic development.
An important element of the LEAD Program is the community based sponsorship. Potential sponsors must demonstrate that they are representative of the whole community and not just of a particular segment. Another important aspect in the development of a community development plan is outlining the steps necessary for overcoming persistent unemployment in the community and how the LEAD program will assist in their implementation.
The LEAD Program will have two components-a project component and a corporation component. The project component provides funds to carry out specific activities related to, (a), enabling a community to prepare an analysis of its current position and a plan for reducing the level of unemployment,
called a planning project; (b), strengthening a community's economic infrastructure within the framework of a local development plan, called the infrastructure project; and (c), creating businesses through community plan development in harmony with regional development strategies, called the enterprise project.
The corporation component has the capacity to provide funds to LEAD corporations which, in turn, provide local businesses with planning technical and professional resources. Corporations will also invest in local businesses so as to result in the creation of new continuing jobs as part of an accepted development plan.
To me, Mr. Speaker, this is a very good program and I am looking forward to seeing communities throughout my area get organized and come forth with representative organizations which will plan and carry out employment development activities that relate directly to the community's own needs and will create permanent jobs.
When one considers the incentives presently under the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion offered to individuals who wish to start a manufacturing or processing business in areas such as South West Nova, one hopes that a combination of the LEAD Program and the Department of Regional and Industrial Expansion will be encouraged to work hand in hand to create permanent employment.
The DR IE Program offers incentives to businesses which wish to modernize or expand. This in itself is very different from the old DREE Program where the grant was for one time. In my view, over the past years this Government's programs have begun to take into account the rural nature of Canada and rural areas such as Southwest Nova.
To return to the Speech from the Throne, I am glad that a new Canada Health Act will be introduced during this session. It should clarify the objectives of Canada's health insurance system and ensure universal access to health care across Canada. Let me point out that we do not have user fees for hospital services in Nova Scotia. The people of our Province should make sure that we do not incorporate such user fees. Medicare should apply to all Canadians, not only to those living in their own Province but to Canadians who visit or wish to move to another province. I know that extra billing for medical services is creating concern. It is going on in Nova Scotia. Medical practitioners in recent years have seen their incomes reduced because of inflation. However, medical fee schedules are a matter for provinces and medical societies to negotiate. Apparently they are not doing this. Provinces may contend that they tolerate extra billing because they do not have enough money to compensate doctors adequately. I ask those provinces, have they really looked at their spending priorities? Perhaps they should state what funds are needed and raise them through general taxation. Introduction of the new Act should bring forth good public discussion on medicare and I look forward to that.
December 12, 1983

Finally, Mr. Speaker, the emphasis in the Speech from the Throne on the single pensioner and the fact that the supplement for single pensioners will be increased is needed. The GIS did not take into account the single pensioner living alone and with expenses similar to those of the two-income pension family. I am glad to see that this injustice will now be remedied for the more than 700,000 single pensioners in Canada. This Government has produced good legislation over the last three and a half years. We have seen the programs and they have been for the benefit of Canadians. The Speech from the Throne gives the direction for this Government to follow. The future is there for all Canadians, and 1 am sure all Canadians will work to make Canada better.

Mr. Speaker, I have a very brief question for the Hon. Member. I listened with considerable interest to her comments, especially as they applied to the fisheries legislation, the restructuring Bill as it was called, Bill C-170. At the time this Bill was debated in the House, examined in committee and brought back to the House for third and final reading I distinctly remember moving two amendments which would have dealt very closely with some of the concerns the Hon. Member expressed today. One dealt with accountability, which would have protected the investment by the Canadian public in this massive monstrosity, this controlling company being established in Atlantic Canada, and the possibility of a second one to be established now in our native Province. 1 ask the Hon. Member why at that time she did not speak out forcefully, as she is endeavouring to do today in support of my amendment?
Second, I would like to know just what happened between November 25, I think it was, when that Bill was given third and final reading, and the present time to make her change her mind and literally condemn the Government, as she is doing, in one breath for bringing in this type of Bill which is restrictive on private companies, and then in the second breath sort of congratulating the Government on the words in the Throne Speech. This puts her in a very contradictory position.
1 would like a further explanation of what happened to her when she got home and the independents contacted her, because obviously something has occurred which is putting her right in the middle of the fence, which is a very awkward position to be in.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is most unfair. He is well aware of the questions I asked witnesses in committee, the speech I made on second reading, and my answer to one of his proposed amendments. 1 have no qualms as far as my constituency goes about my feelings on Bill C-170. However, everyone in this House knows that sometimes there are more powerful forces than one Member of Parliament. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) comes from Central Nova, a small fishing constituency, and he said that they would pass the Bill in one day. We have the NDP, which said at first it was supporting the Bill. At the last minute in the House NDP Members came up and said no, they could not support it because of the banks. My concern was
The Address-Miss Carney
that 1 could not find five Members to stand up and vote on that day because there was an agreement among the parties not to have a vote. I have no qualms in saying that, yes, 1 can represent the concerns of one area in Canada, but there are 281 other Members in this Parliament to be considered. Whether it is a province or a Member of Parliament, I think that is what democracy is, where at least the concerns can be registered.
As far as the Hon. Member's question as to what has happened since is concerned, not too much has happened since. At the last committee hearing, we heard the Deputy Minister from Nova Scotia say that, yes, he wanted guarantees on fish resources written into the agreement between Nova Scotia and the federal Government. We also know that Newfoundland and Nova Scotia want these agreements or they would not be sitting down. There were other ways this could have proceeded. The provinces want these resource allocations for five years to protect the two new supercompanies. That, to me, starts the whole ball rolling where people ask what the Governments are doing in saying how much quota is needed when those companies being restructured have not even been able to manage the quotas they have had for the last number of years. Why did we have the problem to begin with, the soft markets and so on, if they could have marketed good quality fish, all the fish that was out there? Do they need more now in order to make them economically viable? I do not feel that should be written into the agreement.
